extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics instructors (faculty teaching undergraduate math courses)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical classroom assessment and feedback methods for undergraduate mathematics courses, including creating mission statements, soliciting early student feedback, using student feedback teams, and adjusting pedagogy and grading based on findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class mission statement (develop with class)
rubrics_metrics.description: To set the tone of a course at the beginning, develop with the class a “class mission statement,” which can be revisited as the course progresses to assess progress toward meeting course goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the mission statement to align instructor and student expectations, revisit it several times during the term, and use it as a basis for deciding if assignments and processes are meeting class goals. If too diverse, combine common elements into a course-level mission statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial expectation prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific prompts on the first day for students to articulate expectations, e.g. 'Each day I come to class I expect to (be doing)...', 'Each night for homework I expect to (be doing)...', 'Each day I come to class I expect the professor to (be doing)...', 'I expect to do ____ hours of homework between each class', 'I expect my grades to be based on ...', 'If I could get anything out of this class I wanted to, I would make sure that I (got)...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the statements aloud, have students complete them (index cards or post-its), collect and react to them to open dialogue and express instructor expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured PURPOSE / PROCESS / ACCOMPLISHMENTS drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Have students brainstorm and categorize their goals into PURPOSE (why taking the course), PROCESS (how they will fulfill those purposes), and ACCOMPLISHMENTS (specific outcomes/evidence of success).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students write many items (one per card), organize/prioritize, then arrange onto a large sheet in the format: I AM TAKING 'COURSE' (purpose) BY (process) SO THAT (accomplishment). Allow switching statements between categories to fit grammar and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typed take-home reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Require students to take their mission-statement cards home, type them up, and write a paragraph reacting to the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures students re-read and reflect on their statements and deepens engagement with the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic reflection and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect on Mission Statements several times during the semester to check whether chosen goals/processes/accomplishments still work and whether assignments relate to those goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After returning a project, ask students if the assignment pertained to any of their goals, if they used the processes, and whether changes are needed; if processes fail, invite students to propose alternatives or to consult the instructor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesize individual statements into course goals / tailor projects
rubrics_metrics.description: If individual mission statements are too diverse, combine common elements plus any essential unique items into a common Mission Statement for the course; for eliminated individual goals, create individualized projects to help students realize those goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a combined statement to bring in students who wrote shallow statements and use individual projects where necessary to preserve learning opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and time investment for mission statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Create mission statements on the first day or two (not week 3–4) and review after three or four weeks; the initial process takes a full class period and occasional minutes thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to allocate class time (entire period initially) and accept that the time spent is recouped in faster progress later. Do not rush the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor willingness to relinquish control
rubrics_metrics.description: Success increases when the instructor gives more responsibility to students and is willing to relinquish control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect discomfort; traditional control feels difficult to let go. When students and professor work toward the same goals, learning accelerates. Accept the time and behavioral transitions required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use student input to change lecture structure and closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthen mini-lectures to 20–25 minutes, provide end-of-class review and closure, and add demonstrations (e.g., TI-92) as indicated by student input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect informal discussions and e-mail feedback to identify needs for lecture length, demonstration frequency, and closure; implement changes to better prepare students for projects and technology use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide technology training and support
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure students learn basic computer/technology skills (finding and using software like DERIVE, reading menus, authoring statements); provide tutors and assistance in the mathematics laboratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that many students may be new to integrating technology into coursework; provide scaffolding such as tutors, demonstrations, and library/resources (graphing calculators on reserve).

rubrics_metrics.name: Document attendance for retention tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Document class attendance on the first and last day (photographic record) to track retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple records to monitor who remains in the course and correlate retention with interventions or course structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow revision on projects (revision before final grading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of assigning a final grade on first submission, glance through projects to find misconceptions, present anonymized examples to class or create peer review forms, then offer students an opportunity to revise before grading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transparencies or peer-review forms to present common misconceptions; offer one or more revision cycles, grading only after adequate opportunity to improve. This reduces repetitive comments and fosters learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review and use of anonymized class examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Create peer review forms asking students to look for particular misconceptions/lackings in peers' work, or make anonymous copies of misconceptions onto transparencies for class discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review prepares students to critique their own work; transparencies save instructor time and help students identify and fix problems in their own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early in-course anonymous questionnaires
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribute anonymous questionnaires immediately after the first and second exams (approx. weeks 4 and 8) to solicit student feedback on how the class is going and what needs to be changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect, summarize in writing, and discuss the results at the next class; when there is general agreement implement changes; when disagreement occurs, discuss options and vote (thumbs-up/down/side) and solicit reasons to change votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire content categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Design questionnaires with three categories: (1) Attitudinal items (e.g., Likert-scale reactions to cooperative groups), (2) Specific/problematic-area questions (e.g., how to ensure individual accountability in group projects), and (3) Open-response items (likes/dislikes, suggestions, topics difficult to understand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitudinal items are useful after innovations; specific items address problematic logistics; open responses solicit broader input. Use a mix to get actionable and affective data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person-centered approach (Rogers' conditions) in classroom interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Rogers' three core conditions: (1) Unconditional positive regard (value students and trust their capacity), (2) Empathy (understand students' experiences/feelings), (3) Congruence (be genuine in expression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions support a facilitative environment in which students can be trusted to learn and participate responsibly in goal setting and decision making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take student input seriously: summarize and implement promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a written summary of survey results at the next class, discuss possible changes, and implement agreed-upon changes immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students want their input taken seriously; timely summary and implementation increases buy-in. Acknowledge extra instructor time required for surveys and summarization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use feedback to change policies and logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to change grading schemes, group composition, resource allocation, and classroom processes in response to feedback (examples: discard team-average-influenced grading, change groups after exams, institute flexible-weight grading, reserve graphing calculators, allow teams to set process guidelines, design grading for individual accountability, add bonus questions, motivate topics by usefulness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor outcomes of changes (some may not work) and be ready to explain disagreements with class; if whole-class is invested, changes have greatest chance of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-minute paper for end-of-class formative assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quick prompts during the last two minutes of class such as: 'One thing I understand clearly after today’s class is ___.' and 'One thing I wish I had a better understanding of after today’s class is ___.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect these rapid responses as a variant of the One-Minute Paper to identify immediate comprehension and areas needing follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student feedback teams (small representative committee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a student feedback team (e.g., four volunteers with different majors/backgrounds) that meets regularly to assess classroom activities, learning, and homework; use a fact sheet to select a representative group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the team to channel student concerns, suggestions, and to trial modifications. Complement with communication channels such as a listserv and a seating chart containing contact info.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide communication channels for feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish mechanisms for communication (class listserv, seating charts with phone/e-mail/calculator type) so students can direct comments, complaints, and suggestions to the instructor or the feedback committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promise timely responses (e.g., answer all listserv questions before bedtime) to encourage out-of-class dialogue and rapid problem resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time assessment tasks appropriately (after reflection/homework if needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be willing to adapt timing of quick-assessment prompts (e.g., answer One-Minute Paper prompts after students have completed written homework rather than immediately) based on committee feedback about when students can best judge their understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modifying timing can yield more valuable feedback (students may need reflection to know what they understand well or poorly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use brief diagnostic tasks (T/F quizzes) to guide reading and discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Administer short True/False quizzes specific to textbook sections to help students learn how to read a mathematics text and to guide class discussion on troublesome points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect answers as students arrive and use results to focus the day's discussion. Not all students enjoy them, but many find them helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach explicit problem-solving heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide explicit schemes for solving word problems (example seven-point scheme: 1) write the problem in English, 2) construct an 'English-mathematics dictionary', 3) translate into equations, 4) include hidden information and picture data, 5) do calculations, 6) translate answer to English, 7) check answer with initial info and common sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accompany heuristics with detailed examples to remedy common struggles (e.g., time-consuming word problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use feedback to adjust group homework logistics and workload
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust group size (e.g., three instead of four), avoid mixing on-campus and off-campus students in a group, strive for uniform difficulty across assignments, and select a minimal set of exercises to cover situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit committee input about group meeting difficulties and workload variation; implement straightforward logistical changes to increase fairness and manageability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt feedback methods for class size and use supporting tools
rubrics_metrics.description: For larger classes, solicit comments before/after class, use short whole-class discussions without the instructor present, employ student focus groups, and use available software to identify background weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify the feedback mechanism to scale with class size, and use technology (e.g., web/software tools) to help identify and remedy student background deficiencies.
